papers.title: Beyond Infraction Scores: Failure-Boundary Profiles for Closed-Loop Evaluation of Driving and Robot Navigation Agents
papers.authors: Milan Bulat, Gino Ardelean, Ellington Kirby
papers.abstract: Closed-loop driving benchmarks in CARLA rank agents by a driving score that multiplies route completion by an infraction penalty. This score does not distinguish an agent that stops in front of an obstacle from one that pushes past it. In a corridor closed by two parked cars, for example, one agent that drives through with contact averages 52.2 on the blocked widths, while the agents that stop average between 37.8 and 40.6. We propose failure-boundary profiles, an evaluation in which each scenario family varies one measured factor, such as corridor width or the time gap in oncoming traffic, and each variant is certified from measurement as one where the agent should proceed or one where it should stop. Along this axis we estimate two curves per agent, commitment (the probability of attempting the passage) and competence (the probability of passing without contact), and locate where each crosses one half, with intervals that account for the simulator's run-to-run variance. The certified labels also give a summary metric, decision accuracy, which credits clean passes on passable variants and stops on blocked ones. We evaluate seven driving agents on seven CARLA families. The rule-based expert reaches a decision accuracy of 0.74 and TFv6, the highest-scoring learned agent, 0.60. Agents with similar driving scores fail in different ways, and agents that reliably stop at a blocked corridor still rarely wait for a gap in oncoming traffic. We also apply the method, unchanged, to a warehouse robot in Isaac Sim. The navigation policy we test stops at blocked gaps in only one of three families, and two fine-tuned versions of it pass more gaps cleanly but no longer stop at all.

papers.title: BEAKER: An Expert-Curated Benchmark for Embodied Brains in Self-Driving Chemical Laboratories
papers.authors: Fei Lin, Tengchao Zhang, Ziyang Gong, Xiaotong Yu, Bohan Zhang, Yifan Zhou, Qihao Yang, Ji Dai, et al.
papers.abstract: Self-Driving Chemical Laboratories (SDCLs) are moving chemical experimentation toward embodied automation, where machines must perceive laboratory scenes, reason about experimental states, and act under physical, procedural, and safety constraints. Although Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) are increasingly considered as embodied brains for such systems, existing laboratory benchmarks mainly focus on safety, anomaly detection, or general scientific understanding, leaving their execution-oriented embodied capabilities underexplored. To fill this gap, we introduce BEAKER, a Benchmark for evaluating Embodied Actionability, Knowledge, Experimentation, and Reasoning in SDCLs. BEAKER contains 1,000 expert-curated question-answer samples across 11 image and video task types, covering key judgments required for chemical laboratory execution, including affordance grounding, trajectory planning, equipment, state, and safety recognition, apparatus setup, operation and step reasoning, and temporal procedure reasoning. All questions and annotations are manually created and reviewed by chemistry and embodied Artificial Intelligence (AI) experts, without AI-assisted generation or annotation. We evaluate 28 general-purpose, science-oriented, chemistry-specialized, and embodied MLLMs in an offline, single-turn setting. Results show that current models can follow coarse experimental procedures in videos, but still struggle to ground actions into operable regions and feasible trajectories, to recognize fine-grained laboratory apparatus, states, and safety norms, and to order steps in mid-length procedures. BEAKER thus reveals a clear gap between coarse procedural understanding and the precise, action-grounded perception required for laboratory execution, providing a diagnostic benchmark for future MLLMs in SDCLs.

papers.title: Agentic AI and related systems in nursing and nursing-adjacent work: a scoping review of task allocation, decision authority, and accountability
papers.authors: Rabie Adel El Arab, Mohammad Hussein Mustafa, Sarah AlFehaid, Sammanah Mohammed Alturaiki, Mudassir Imran Mustafa
papers.abstract: Introduction Agentic artificial intelligence (AI) and related systems are being investigated for nursing and nursing-adjacent work, but inconsistent terminology and heterogeneous evaluations obscure their operational capabilities and clinical relevance. This review examined the relationship between reported agentic behavior, evaluation in nursing practice, retained decision authority, and evidence concerning patient benefit, workload, and accountability. Methods We conducted a scoping review informed by JBI guidance and reported in accordance with PRISMA-ScR. We searched PubMed, Embase, CINAHL, Scopus, and Web of Science, supplemented by citation and linked-report searching. Results Among 28 reports, 13 satisfied all criteria, four were indeterminate, and 11 lacked at least one criterion. Only two qualifying reports evaluated live nurse–AI workflows. Nursing participation ranged from clinical work to education, co-design, output rating, and outcome assessment, and did not uniformly represent runtime control. Patient-facing clinical workflows retained professional decision authority; robotics evaluations involved neither nurses nor patients. Outcomes principally concerned technical performance, communication, usability, or component-specific efficiency. The evidence did not establish autonomous nursing practice, sustained patient benefit, or reduced complete-episode nursing workload. No empirical evaluation of accountability or redress following AI-related error was identified. Discussion Operational qualification, clinical benefit, and accountable use require separate evaluation. Future studies should assess the complete human–AI pathway, including verification, correction, escalation, patient outcomes, and responses to failure. Comparative designs should isolate agentic mechanisms from additional computation, information access, and workflow redesign. A proposed post hoc , unvalidated heuristic links allocated function, decision authority, assurance, and accountability/redress. Interpretation is limited by absent prospective registration, unquantified agreement before consensus, related reports, and the absence of formal risk-of-bias assessment. Conclusion Agentic capability alone does not establish clinical readiness. Expanding AI-enabled functions requires evidence of meaningful benefit, effective human control, and accountability arrangements proportionate to the consequences of system actions.

papers.title: Adaptive Hybrid Force-Vision Control with EMG-Derived References for Deformable Bottle Manipulation
papers.authors: Jeffrey Lee, Geoffrey Hanks, Evangeline Bouganim, Yue Hu
papers.abstract: Robotic automation of laboratory tasks has become a growing interest to remove researchers from hazardous environments and repetitive procedures. However, even equipment as simple as squeeze bottles poses a challenging manipulation problem due to its deformability. This paper presents an adaptive hybrid vision-force controller for robotic grippers to effectively manipulate laboratory squeeze bottles to dispense liquid. This approach integrates force and vision feedback according to the interaction state, enabling effective squeezing while accounting for bottle deformation and recovery. The proposed controller is validated by comparing its performance with a pure force controller on 12 combinations of conditions consisting of 2 target dispense volumes, 2 plastic squeeze bottles, and 1 to 3 squeezes used to dispense. Human demonstrations of these operating conditions were collected using electromyography (EMG) sensing mapped to a desired grip force, which was then used as the force reference for the controllers to squeeze the bottles. Results demonstrated that the proposed adaptive hybrid vision-force controller achieved more accurate liquid dispensing with a mean absolute error (MAE) of 6.54 mL compared to a MAE of 15.92 mL from the pure force controller, while also replicating the human action recorded from the EMG signal more closely.

papers.title: AI-Driven Business: Transforming Business Operations, Decision-Making and Future Growth
papers.authors: Shraddha Shraddha
papers.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has become one of the most important technological developments in the modern business environment. It is changing the way organisations operate, communicate with customers, make decisions, manage employees and compete in the marketplace. An AI-driven business is an organisation that uses artificial intelligence technologies to improve its business processes, increase productivity, reduce operating costs and create better customer experiences. Technologies such as machine learning, natural language processing, robotics, predictive analytics, computer vision and generative AI are being used in different business activities. These technologies help companies analyse large amounts of data, predict customer behaviour, automate repetitive tasks, manage inventory, detect financial fraud and develop innovative products and services. The purpose of this research paper is to study the meaning, importance, applications, benefits and challenges of AI-driven businesses. It also examines how artificial intelligence is influencing different business functions, including marketing, finance, human resource management, production, customer service and supply chain management. Special attention is given to the development of AI-driven businesses in India and the opportunities available to Indian companies. The research is based on secondary information collected from government publications, research reports, academic resources and international organisations. The study finds that AI can improve business efficiency and competitiveness, but its successful implementation requires proper planning, skilled employees, reliable data, financial investment and ethical practices. The paper concludes that artificial intelligence is not simply a technological tool but an important part of the future business strategy.

papers.title: A scientometric and bibliometric analysis of three decades of global robotics and Internet of Things research trends and intellectual structure
papers.authors: Reetu Verma, Kavita Pabreja
papers.abstract: The convergence of robotics and the Internet of Things (IoT) has transformed multiple sectors through autonomous, interconnected systems. Despite significant scholarly output, the knowledge structure of Robotics-IoT research remains fragmented. This study provides an integrated scientometric and bibliometric mapping of global Robotics–IoT/IoRT research, combining performance analysis, collaboration-network mapping, thematic mapping, and LDA-based topic modelling to reveal the field’s intellectual structure, collaboration architecture, dominant clusters, emerging themes, and future research frontiers. A scientometric analysis was conducted on 21,733 unique documents retrieved from Scopus and Web of Science after screening and deduplication of 23,377 initial records, covering 1993–2025 across 2,284 sources and over 44,000 indexed author-name records/clusters, cleaned via the PRISMA protocol. Biblioshiny and VOSviewer were employed for publication trends, citation structures, and collaborative networks, while LDA was applied for topic modelling. Robotics-IoT research shows rapid growth post-2016. Using all-author affiliation-country document-level full counting, India, China, and the USA lead publication output. Among the ten most productive countries, Australia shows the highest average citations per document, followed by Canada, the USA, and the United Kingdom. Collaboration networks reflect extensive global partnerships, with emerging economies demonstrating substantial international participation. Thematic analysis identifies major research streams related to industrial digitalization, IoT–robotic systems, energy-efficient networking, machine-learning-based analytics, robotics and sensing, cybersecurity, and edge/cloud computing, alongside specialized applications in agriculture and healthcare. Observed distributions show varying degrees of descriptive alignment with classical scientometric laws (Lotka’s, Bradford’s, Price’s, Zipf’s, Matthew Effect, and Pareto Principle). The originality of this study lies in the domain-specific application and empirical synthesis of these approaches to the global Robotics–IoT/IoRT research landscape. Specifically, the study provides a longitudinal analysis covering 1993–2025, examines the intellectual, social, publication and thematic structures of the Robotics–IoT/IoRT domain, evaluates a comparatively broad set of classical scientometric regularities, and complements keyword-based analysis with abstract-based LDA topic modelling. The study consequently contributes new empirical evidence concerning the evolution, concentration, collaboration, intellectual structure and thematic development of Robotics–IoT/IoRT research.

papers.title: A human-centric large language model interface for monitoring and control of autonomous mobile robots via digital twins in industry 5.0
papers.authors: Ján Piteľ, Kamil Židek, Nino Natmeladze
papers.abstract: The diversity of industrial robot manufacturers, proprietary programming languages, and graphical interfaces complicates robotic system deployment and operation. This heterogeneity highlights the need for intuitive, accessible, and human-centric interaction methods. This paper presents a framework for natural language-based monitoring and selected control of autonomous mobile robots using a Large Language Model (LLM) interface, structured API communication, and digital twin visualization. The approach enables operators to interact with robots through natural language without requiring detailed knowledge of robot-specific interfaces or technical commands. The framework is evaluated from the operator’s perspective, focusing on its ability to simplify access to robot information, reduce interaction complexity, and support selected control tasks. Digital twin integration provides additional visual feedback on robot status and its operating environment. The proposed framework contributes to the development of more transparent, accessible, and human-oriented robotic systems aligned with Industry 5.0 principles.

papers.title: A Timeline of Clinical Applications of Robots in Cranial Neurosurgery
papers.authors: Miss Anjum Aarifa Khanom, Callum Ward, Joseph Davids, Arup Ray, Aprajay Golash, Andrew Folusho Alalade
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: A robot is a reprogrammable multifunctional manipulator designed to move tools through varied motions. In surgery, robots have been introduced for their tireless operation, precision, and consistency. However, the use of cranial neurosurgical robots remains in its infancy. METHODS: A literature search was conducted in PubMed, Medline and Google Scholar. This search focused on the first clinical applications of robotics in cranial neurosurgery to date. A manual search was also conducted. RESULTS: Twenty robotic systems were identified. Sixteen were passive devices primarily used for stereotactic neurosurgery. Shared and supervisory-controlled robots are increasing in prevalence due to technological advances. Eight systems are commercially available, highlighting their success in meeting clinical needs. CONCLUSION: It is apparent that the landscape is dominated by stereotactic robots with passive functioning. There is an increasing prevalence of active and shared-control systems. Advancements in technology, cost and learning curve remain barriers to the scalability of neurosurgical robots.

papers.title: A Layered View of LLM Support in Underwater Robotics
papers.authors: Federico Celi, Leonardo Zacchini, Gabriele Ferri
papers.abstract: This extended abstract discusses a specific and, in our experience, practically relevant role for large language models (LLMs) in underwater robotics. Our main premise is that, in underwater fielding missions, the immediate difficulty is often not the synthesis of new low-level control laws, but the operation of complex robotic systems under limited communications, partial observability, and expensive field time. In particular, a significant fraction of the effort during sea trials is devoted to fault diagnosis, telemetry interpretation, mission adjustment, and coordination across heterogeneous assets and operators. We argue that LLMs may be useful at this higher operational level, especially when grounded in structured vehicle state, alarms, logs, mission context, and existing planning or validation tools. At the same time, current limitations in grounding, consistency, and causal reasoning make these systems lack the predictability required to guarantee direct control, especially in real-world critical applications, although we do not exclude a future evolution in this direction. This viewpoint suggests a layered architecture in which conventional autonomy remains responsible for control, perception, estimation, and validated mission execution, whereas LLM-based modules serve as an additional support layer for debugging, operator interaction, constrained replanning support, orchestration, and post-mission analysis.

papers.title: $A^3$-VLA: Automatic Perception-Guided Attention Alignment for Robot Manipulation
papers.authors: Shengzhe Zhang, Qi Zhang, Dazhong Shen, Chao Wang, Shaopeng Zhai, Hui Xiong
papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action Models (VLAs) enable robots to perform manipulation tasks by leveraging Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to process visual observations and language instructions. However, the action prediction objective itself lacks fine-grained task-specific perceptual supervision, making it prone to relying on task-irrelevant visual shortcuts, leading attention away from target objects and key interaction areas, thereby limiting its operational performance and generalization ability. To address this, we propose Automatic Perception-Guided Attention Alignment for Robot Manipulation ($A^3$-VLA), a framework that derives task-specific visual guidance from the manipulation process itself. Specifically, $A^3$-VLA first generates heuristic candidate regions for target objects and the robot from interaction-induced visual changes, and refines them with a visual segmentation model offline. These regions serve as explicit perceptual guidance through two complementary objectives: an attention allocation loss that encourages sufficient focus on task-critical regions when language or robot state tokens query the visual input, and a contrastive learning loss that aligns the representations of candidate target regions with language instructions while separating them from task-irrelevant regions. Extensive experiments on simulated and real-world manipulation tasks demonstrate that $A^3$-VLA consistently improves multiple VLA backbones, with an average success rate gain of 6.5% - 25.2% across benchmarks.

papers.title: iMED: A Multi-Endoscope Dataset for Surgical 3D Perception
papers.authors: Sierra Bonilla, Fengyi Jiang, Chinedu Nwoye, Jingpei Lu, Kailey Reardon, Humphrey W. Chow, Francisco Vasconcelos, Sophia Bano, et al.
papers.abstract: We introduce iMED, the first synchronized multi-endoscope dataset for robot-assisted minimally invasive surgery (RAMIS), designed to address a fundamental limitation in surgical vision benchmarking: the absence of independent held-out viewpoints. Existing surgical datasets capture single-trajectory sequences from a single endoscope, making it impossible to distinguish geometric generalization from photometric interpolation along a narrow forward-facing path. iMED provides 340 sequences ~170K synchronized timepoints with 4 views per timepoint) recorded simultaneously from two independent stereo endoscopes across ex vivo, postmortem, and live surgical settings, spanning 14 specimens with diverse anatomical regions and motion regimes. The dataset includes calibrated camera intrinsics, ArUco-based frame-wise pose estimates with uncertainty quantification, instrument segmentation masks, and rich clinical metadata. Using a train-on-one-endoscope, test-on-another evaluation protocol, we benchmark 23 state-of-the-art methods across rigid and deformable novel view synthesis, pose estimation, feature matching, and monocular depth estimation. Our experiments show that methods relying primarily on photometric supervision degrade substantially under this held-out-endoscope setting, while methods with explicit geometric regularization are more robust across views in our benchmark. Notably, large-scale foundation models transfer surprisingly well to surgical imagery, often outperforming domain-specific models, suggesting pitfalls in current fine-tuning protocols. iMED establishes a new evaluation protocol for geometric generalization in surgical vision.

papers.title: When Physical AI Gets Hacked: From Software Exploits to Kinetic Catastrophe and the 25ns Hardware Remedy
papers.authors: Steven K
papers.abstract: QuantNature Technical Brief Series (Vol. 2)Document ID: QN-TB-2026-002Publication Date: November 2026 Executive Summary As artificial intelligence transitions from digital screens into embodied Physical AI—powering autonomous humanoids, industrial mobile robotics (AGVs/AMRs), and high-voltage electric vehicle powertrains—the vulnerability landscape shifts decisively from informational data theft to catastrophic kinetic sabotage. Conventional cybersecurity relies entirely on software-level isolation, kernel privilege rings, and cryptographic handshakes (SELinux, eBPF, ROS 2 SROS) operating within the non-deterministic timing domain of host operating systems. When an operating system is breached via zero-day exploits, supply-chain attacks, or generative AI model hallucinations, all software-based guards collapse, granting adversaries unfettered authority to command physical actuators directly. While industry standards mandate binary Safe Torque Off (STO) circuits to physically cut gate power during faults, severing torque in mobile Physical AI induces catastrophic dynamic collapse, vehicle rollover, and irreversible operational halting. This Technical Brief analyzes the structural roots of this kinetic vulnerability and presents the architectural blueprint for an in-line, sub-cycle hardware interlock positioned directly at the actuator boundary. Operating at a deterministic 25.0 ns single-clock registered pipeline (40.00 MHz), this physical-layer governor decouples high-level command formulation from low-level kinetic execution, enforcing immutable physical stability corridors and establishing an authoritative framework for hardware-rooted robot safety. Key Technical Findings The Semantic Blindness of Conventional Motor DSPs: Specialized 32-bit digital signal processors (such as the TI C2000 family, STM32, or Infineon AURIX) execute field-oriented control (FOC) under total semantic blindness. They verify cyclic redundancy checks (CRC) and packet framing, yet faithfully drive the power inverter into destructive saturation upon receiving malicious out-of-bounds torque commands. They protect against transmission noise, not malicious intent. The Safe-Torque-Off (STO) Dilemma: Abruptly severing actuator power destroys dynamic equilibrium in bipedal humanoids, quadrupeds, and drones, precipitating fatal gravitational crashes. Furthermore, STO acts as an irreversible trip latch requiring manual human power-cycling—preventing a hijacked machine from defending itself without committing operational suicide. In-Line Sub-Cycle Silicon Gatekeeping (τcore = 25.0 ns): Interposed as an un-bypassable hardware air-gap between the host bus (AXI/PCIe) and the peripheral PWM gate-drive registers, dedicated FPGA/silicon fabric intercepts candidate duty cycles and validates physical feasibility at single-clock speed (τcore = 25.0 ns ≪ Tsw), eliminating software-dependent latency floors (1,795–5,000 ns). Empirical Telemetric Validation: Across a 40.00 kHz PWM power stage under acute command injections, when an adversary commands a persistent 95.0% motor kill duty under high-entropy noise, the hardware interlock autonomously clamps the output strictly within a reconfigurable safe physical corridor (< 12.0%) with zero limit-cycle chattering (0 Hz), completely arresting mechanical gear shearing and kinetic runaway at the silicon layer. This technical brief establishes that software security alone cannot safeguard physical actuators, providing the foundational hardware-governed architecture required for safe, insurable, and sovereign Physical AI.

papers.title: WayTrace: A Map-to-Language-to-Trace Hierarchy for Embodied Urban Navigation
papers.authors: Manthan Patel, Jonas Frey, Pascal Roth, Marco Hutter, Cesar Cadena
papers.abstract: Web services provide walking directions for nearly every city, but following them reliably over long routes remains challenging for autonomous robots. Point-goal navigation policies rely heavily on accurate GNSS, while most vision-language navigation models struggle to execute even short instructions outdoors. We present WayTrace, a hierarchical system that connects web-map directions to robot motion through language. An off-the-shelf orchestrator vision-language model reads the turn-by-turn directions, a satellite map and recent camera images, and issues one atomic language command at a time, such as "cross the road to the left". An onboard trace predictor, trained on over one million automatically labelled samples from street-level images, draws the path for this command in the image, and a reinforcement learning policy tracks it. In long-range simulated missions, WayTrace remains robust to GNSS noise and rarely leaves crosswalks or sidewalks, while point-goal baselines degrade sharply with about ten times more violations. Deployed on a wheeled-legged robot, WayTrace completes real-world missions of up to 1.37 km at about 1.1 m/s through a busy city centre, rural trails and a university campus, handling crosswalks, staircases and construction sites. Project page: https://way-trace.github.io

papers.title: Trusting Imagined Futures: Auditing Imagined Rewards for VLA Post-Training
papers.authors: Zicheng Kong, Zhenbo Xu, Haoyan Zhang, Jinghan Yang, Zhenzhen Li, Yiwei Ru, Liuyu Xiang, WanTing Xu, et al.
papers.abstract: Video world models enable candidate actions to be evaluated through imagined outcomes, but high predicted rewards can favor trajectories with poor execution quality. We introduce Trusting Imagined Futures (TIF), an offline supervision selection method for vision-language-action (VLA) post-training that audits predicted rewards using execution feedback. A multidimensional reward model predicts a utility score for candidate ranking and five dimensions of execution quality. An auditor uses reward predictions and uncertainty to identify overestimation patterns learned from paired imagined videos and real executions. TIF accepts the candidate with the highest predicted utility when its advantage over the existing trajectory exceeds a margin and its audit risk passes a threshold; otherwise, it retains the existing supervision. The retained real trajectories then supervise behavior cloning. Across four LIBERO suites and three training seeds, TIF achieves a mean success rate of 76.25%, improving over training on the existing trajectories by 3.00 percentage points with the same trajectory count and training budget. Adding audit gating yields 1.47 percentage points with the reward model and advantage margin held fixed. The gains persist against advantage ranking and logistic regression risk selection at matched replacement counts. On recorded videos from three real robot tasks, TIF increases clean completion among selected trajectories from 58.33% to 70.00% across 60 candidate pools.

papers.title: Trajectory Evaluation via Rollout-Free World Model for End-to-end Autonomous Driving
papers.authors: Junzhe Wang, Jinqing Zhang, Qingjie Liu
papers.abstract: Although existing candidate trajectory evaluators have substantially improved end-to-end planning accuracy, their underlying mechanism remains suboptimal. Model-based evaluators typically make scoring future-aware by explicitly predicting candidate-conditioned future states over the planning horizon, which we term rollout. However, rollout incurs high inference cost and accumulates prediction errors. We argue that planning does not require reconstructing a full future scene for each candidate, but only future-relevant information for reliable comparison. We therefore propose RFWorld, a Rollout-Free World model for end-to-end trajectory evaluation. RFWorld constructs a shared scene memory and shapes it into a future-readable representation via lightweight training-time temporal readout with semantic supervision, keeping training overhead low. At inference time, candidate trajectories directly query the shared memory via sparse spatial readout for scoring, reducing computation by roughly the planning horizon times the number of candidate trajectories, while avoiding recursive rollout errors. Experiments on NAVSIM and Bench2Drive show that RFWorld learns a more planning-aligned world representation and achieves state-of-the-art performance.

papers.title: Synthesizing Dexterous Robot Demonstrations from Human Videos via Virtual Try-On
papers.authors: Seungyong Lee, Suhyeok Jang, Minyoung Kim, Jinwoo Shin
papers.abstract: Robot foundation models have shown remarkable performance in robot control, yet adapting them to a new task still relies heavily on teleoperated demonstrations. Egocentric human videos offer a scalable substitute, but overlaying rendered robots on human videos or retargeting human poses into robot actions leaves significant visual or action gaps for high-DoF robot embodiments. To address this limitation, we propose RoboTryOn, which treats human-to-robot translation as virtual try-on: try-on keeps the person and swaps the garment, RoboTryOn keeps the demonstrated motion and swaps the human for the robot. Specifically, RoboTryOn converts a human video into a video of the target robot specified by a reference image, while preserving the original task, objects, and background. To maintain visual consistency, we translate selected keyframes autoregressively and use them to guide video synthesis with motion conditioned on the human hand skeleton. Additionally, we use an inverse dynamics model (IDM) that incorporates depth features to infer action labels from synthesized videos for policy learning. Our experiments across multiple humanoid embodiments show that policies trained with our synthetic data improve the average success rate on novel tasks, including challenging bimanual manipulation, from 2% to 60%, without any real robot demonstration of those tasks. Moreover, training with our synthetic data matches the performance of policies trained solely on teleoperated demonstrations at approximately a third of the collection cost, demonstrating the cost efficiency of our approach.

papers.title: SurgTransfer: Multi-Step Latent Action Modeling for Action Transfer in Surgical World Model
papers.authors: Saurabh Koju, Love Panta, Deepak Thapa, Rudra P. K. Poudel, Prajwal Ghimire, Angus Watson, Yash Raj Shrestha, Prashnna Kumar Gyawali, et al.
papers.abstract: Surgical world models have the potential to provide intra-operative guidance, accelerate risk-free training and facilitate transfer of expert surgical maneuvers. However, the use of world models for transferring surgical expertise has been largely unexplored. Moreover, recent approaches in this domain have mainly relied on ground truth kinematics actions or expert annotations for specific tasks, limiting their applicability beyond the narrow range of tasks with ground-truth annotations. In contrast, existing works in the natural domain have shown promising results in learning latent actions solely from unlabeled videos and transferring the learned actions across contexts. We observe that this paradigm is short-sighted for the surgical domain, failing to capture the hierarchical and goal-directed structure of surgical procedures. Thus, we propose a novel multi-step action learning framework to learn context-invariant latent actions that are easily transferable across various surgical contexts. We perform extensive experiments on the publicly available datasets, SurgToolLoc-2022 and PitVis-2023, verifying our approach with both quantitative metrics and qualitative evaluation by surgical experts. We have published our code and the implementation details at https://github.com/bhattarailab/Surgical-Vision-World-Model.

papers.title: Spectrally Routed Diffusion Policy for Multi-Task Robotic Manipulation
papers.authors: Mingcong Li, Yihan Zhou, Jiayu Qu, Xueyang Guo, Yilin Mo
papers.abstract: Diffusion-based policies have achieved strong performance on single-task robotic manipulation. However, a single model trained jointly on multiple tasks consistently underperforms the per-task specialists trained on the same demonstrations. We focus on two challenges. First, the convolutional encoders commonly used in diffusion-based policies produce visual conditions that are not discriminative enough. Second, gradients from incompatible action modes update the shared denoiser's dense parameters along the same directions, causing destructive interference during joint training. To address both, we propose SR-DP (Spectrally Routed Diffusion Policy). A frozen VGGT encoder with a spatial-compression adapter produces compact multi-scale semantic-geometric tokens, a task-discriminative visual condition for tasks that share a workspace. We first train the denoiser as a standard diffusion policy, then decompose selected linear layers by SVD into a frozen basis of orthogonal rank-one experts, adapted through spectral routing and Householder input rotations. On six RoboTwin tasks, SR-DP averages a 68.4% success rate, surpassing multi-task VO-DP by 21.8 points and the strongest per-task baseline by 3.8 points. On four real-world bimanual tasks, Stage 2 reaches a 43.0% average success rate and improves over Stage 1 by 19.0 points.

papers.title: Sparse Anchors for Visual Multi-Session Registration in Changing Environments
papers.authors: Yunus Talha Erzurumlu, Niklas Trekel, Saurabh Gupta, Nico Koltermann, Olga Vysotska, Jens Behley, Louis Wiesmann, Cyrill Stachniss
papers.abstract: Repeated robotic monitoring requires localization across visits to the same environment, even if the environment changes. Such changes can substantially reduce persistent visual content, and repetitive structures can lead to incorrect cross-session correspondences. In this paper, we address visual multi-session registration of a new data recording (the query session) to a previously reconstructed reference map. Under substantial visual and structural changes, cross-session localization may be possible only for parts of the trajectory. In our approach, we therefore rely on a sparse set of reliable absolute pose constraints and combine them with within-session relative-pose information to register the complete trajectory to the reference map. We first estimate absolute alignment hypotheses through visual place recognition, local feature matching, and geometric verification. We then use sequence consensus to reject hypotheses that are inconsistent with a common query-to-reference alignment and retain the remaining poses as absolute anchors. These anchors are refined through featuremetric alignment against a Gaussian feature field and combined with within-session relative-pose constraints in a robust pose-graph optimization. We evaluate our approach on 15 cross-session experiments from the challenging HILTI26 construction-site dataset, covering substantial scene changes and difficult-to-match environments. Our method achieves 94.4% recall within 1m and 100.0% within 5m, outperforming independent image localization, which peaks at 65.3% and 70.7%, respectively, as well as direct registration of independently reconstructed Structure-from-Motion geometry. Our results show that sparse, reliable absolute anchors can provide accurate and complete trajectory registration even when reliable cross-session correspondences are available only for part of the query session.

papers.title: Should the Action Expert Train the VLM? Action-Token Supervision and Gradient Routing in Mixture-of-Transformer VLAs
papers.authors: Asher James Hancock, Boyi Li, Yuxiao Chen, Shuhan Tan, Wenhao Ding, Thomas Tian, Yan Wang, Boris Ivanovic, et al.
papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models increasingly pair a pre-trained vision-language model (VLM) with a flow-matching expert that conditions its action predictions on the VLM's key-value representations. Those representations must carry information useful for control, yet the VLM was never trained for the action expert's flow-matching objective. Two signals can address this: gradients backpropagated from the expert's loss (coupling), or VLM supervision to predict discrete tokens encoding the same target actions. Prominent training recipes forgo the first, blocking expert-to-VLM gradients (insulation) to protect the VLM's existing capabilities, while also supervising it on vision-language data and action tokens. Because vision-language co-training also aims to preserve those capabilities, the additional protection provided by insulation is unclear. At the same time, insulation removes a direct signal about which features continuous action prediction requires. On the other hand, action-token supervision offers an alternative way to learn action-relevant representations, which may explain why insulation succeeds in practice. We disentangle these factors in autonomous driving and manipulation by independently varying action-token supervision and whether the expert's loss updates the VLM. In open-loop driving, insulation is competitive with coupling when action tokens are supervised; without them, coupling reduces trajectory-prediction error by roughly 25%. When both components are trained jointly from the outset, coupling increases closed-loop driving route progress by approximately 17% with action-token supervision and 40% without it, and similarly improves robot manipulation performance under both settings. These findings show that the value of gradient insulation depends on the VLM's action supervision and the evaluation setting, challenging insulation as a default VLA training recipe.

papers.title: SettleSplat: Monocular Gaussian Mapping under In-View Scene Changes
papers.authors: Anh Thuan Tran, Xiyun Song, Yubin Zhou, Heather Yu, Jana Kosecka, Liang Peng
papers.abstract: Online 3D Gaussian mapping enables fast and high-fidelity novel view synthesis, with broad applications in augmented reality, robotics, and autonomous systems. However, many current methods assume static scenes or filter out dynamics as outliers. In this paper, we study in-view scene changes where objects are manipulated in front of the camera within a single online sequence, unlike prior works that detect changes outside the camera view or between separate captures. This setting entangles transient and persistent dynamics, as objects can be distractors while moving and persistent once they settle. While recent studies start to address distractors by removing them for clean static background, in-view scene changes remain underexplored. To resolve this, we present SettleSplat, a monocular mapping system that maintains up-to-date 3D Gaussian maps under such changes. Specifically, we lift coarse per-pixel uncertainty into Gaussian dynamicity field, then prune transient ones. For persistent changes, we derive geometric contradictions weighted by parameter-free rendered depth uncertainty to separate true changes from under-optimized regions. On Bonn and Co-Fusion, SettleSplat achieves consistent 3D Gaussian maps, outperforming current baselines on both full images and change regions while maintaining comparable speed.

papers.title: Say the Same, Act Differently: Diagnosing and Steering Text-Action Divergence in Reasoning VLAs
papers.authors: Zihao Feng, Qingzhao Zhang, Chunyu Xia, Bo Yu, Z. Morley Mao, Ramesh Govindan
papers.abstract: Reasoning vision-language-action (VLA) models pair physical control with natural-language rationales that supervisors can read to monitor embodied safety. Prior attacks on VLA reasoning corrupt the rationale itself and leave visible evidence in the text. We show that visual perturbations can instead alter the physical action while keeping the generated rationale word-for-word identical. At the shared text/action interface of Alpamayo for driving and InstructVLA for manipulation, our text-neutral action-subspace (TNAS) diagnostic shows that the locally most action-sensitive direction is nearly orthogonal to the active text-loss gradients, with 1.87% and 5.28% norm overlap. At equal hidden-state perturbation norms across both models, interventions along this text-neutral residual shift actions 4.64x to 47.8x more than text-gradient perturbations, whereas text-gradient perturbations induce 21.2x to 277x more text drift. Steering visual perturbations along this direction reaches the same decoupling from the image. Across 154 obstacle-annotated driving scenes in Alpamayo, TNAS-guided attacks induce a new collision under a word-for-word identical rationale in 52.6% of scenes under full-image perturbations and 35.1% under a localized forward-camera patch, compared with 4.55% for unguided action attacks. Relative to a text-preserving baseline, TNAS guidance raises exact rationale preservation from 83.0% to 89.5% and cuts teacher-forced text drift by 68.4% at a comparable collision rate. In InstructVLA, TNAS guidance cuts text drift by 40.5% and preserves the exact response on 85.0% of examples alongside a 1.73-unit action-chunk shift. An unchanged rationale therefore cannot certify a safe action, so monitors for reasoning VLAs must verify the predicted action channel directly.

papers.title: SPOD: Recovering Suppressed Temporal Evidence in Video-LLMs via Single-Pass Orthogonal Decomposition
papers.authors: Yangguang Lin, Quan Fang, Xiaoyan Liu, Zefan Xu
papers.abstract: Video Large Language Models (Video-LLMs) have achieved strong performance on many video understanding tasks, yet remain vulnerable to temporal hallucination in time-sensitive reasoning scenarios such as scene transition understanding and event ordering. Existing solutions either require costly retraining or introduce inefficient multi-pass inference and external supervision at test time. In this work, we show that temporal evidence is already encoded in Video-LLM hidden representations but is not fully exploited during standard inference. Motivated by this observation, we propose Single-Pass Orthogonal Decomposition (SPOD), a training-free framework that recovers suppressed temporal evidence through analytical hidden-state manipulation in a single forward pass. SPOD consists of two components: Frame Distinctiveness Analysis (FDA), which identifies salient frames from middle-layer hidden-state geometry, and Temporal Delta Subspace (TDS), which constructs orthogonal temporal and prior subspaces from weighted inter-frame hidden-state differences. By decomposing final hidden states into temporal, prior, and residual components and rescaling them independently, SPOD enhances dynamic information, suppresses static appearance bias, and preserves complementary information. Experiments on VidHalluc, EventHallusion, and VideoMMMU show that SPOD consistently outperforms strong inference-time baselines across temporal reasoning tasks and model architectures while retaining near-vanilla inference efficiency. These results suggest that improving temporal reasoning in Video-LLMs may depend not only on additional supervision, but also on recovering temporal evidence already present in their internal representations. Our code is available at https://github.com/VioAgnes/SPOD.

papers.title: Route Anything: A Study of Model and Policy Routing for General-Purpose AI Systems
papers.authors: Pengfei Zhou, Yixing Ma, Hexin Wang, Weidong Tang, Zhenglin Wan, Wangbo Zhao, Yang You
papers.abstract: Artificial general intelligence (AGI) requires a method that can understand, generate, reason, and act across diverse domains and modalities. Rather than relying on a single model to master every capability, a promising path toward AGI now is to orchestrate a heterogeneous ecosystem of specialized models, tools, and policies (candidates) into a unified AI system. At the heart of this vision lies a fundamental question: how can an AI system dynamically select and coordinate the most capable candidate for each task while balancing performance and computational cost? In this work, we present Route Anything, a unified framework for studying model and policy routing across general-purpose AI systems. We develop a unified theoretical foundation that characterizes optimal routing under quality--cost trade-offs and establishes how the information available to a router determines its attainable performance. To systematically investigate routing across diverse capabilities, we first construct an omni-modal trajectory matrix spanning 25 benchmarks across language understanding, image, video, and speech generation, coding and workplace agents, and robotic manipulation, comprising 374,401 scored runs from 452 candidate configurations. Building on this framework, we train and test different routers to investigate the potential of omni-modal model routing, the capabilities of learned routers, and the conditions under which routing improves efficiency. Our results reveal substantial opportunities for capability orchestration: per-input oracle routing outperforms the best fixed candidate by 5.4 points, and learned routers outperform it by 0.3 points across 16 benchmarks, by 2.1 points on video generation, and by 1.1 points on robot manipulation while using 24% less policy time. More importantly, routing raises efficiency by 8.82x on average compared with the reference model.

papers.title: Role-based Effectiveness of an Epistemic Uncertainty Estimate in Training Models for Semantic Segmentation of 3D LiDAR Point Clouds
papers.authors: Krishnakumar N, Jaya Sreevalsan-Nair
papers.abstract: Point cloud segmentation is a fundamental task in 3D data analysis, with applications across robotics, augmented and virtual reality, and remote sensing. However, the inherent sparsity, noise, and unordered nature of point clouds introduce significant challenges, particularly in achieving reliable classification. While the state-of-the-art rely on training models for explicit modeling of uncertainty, there is a gap in exploring different roles that estimated uncertainty using generative approaches can play. This work investigates the impact of deterministic uncertainty in point cloud segmentation by explicitly modeling epistemic uncertainty and using it in different roles, namely, as a feature and in loss function. We evaluate a baseline artificial neural network (ANN) and two uncertainty-aware variants (uncertainty as an additional input feature and as a per-sample confidence weight in the training loss) on four large-scale LiDAR benchmarks spanning airborne and mobile acquisition, namely ISPRS Vaihingen, AHN3, Paris-Lille-3D, and Toronto-3D, together with PointNet++ and RandLA-Net references and their uncertainty-augmented counterparts under canonical spatially disjoint train and test splits. Under this protocol, uncertainty-aware modeling improves mean Intersection over Union, recovers minority classes that the baseline ANN never predicts at all, and in half of the configurations improves the alignment between prediction error and estimated uncertainty as measured by Patch Accuracy versus Patch Uncertainty. Our findings indicate that uncertainty can play multiple roles in the segmentation pipeline rather than as a device for improving accuracy alone.

papers.title: ReflexArc: Bottom-Up Integration of Instantaneous Tactile Reflexes into Whole-Body Humanoid Control
papers.authors: Mingyu Wang, Si Li, Ziqing Chen, He Wang, Li Yi
papers.abstract: Humanoid robots operating in cluttered environments must react to unexpected contacts before the first impact peak, which arrives within tens of milliseconds. Learned whole-body policies running at 50 Hz introduce a policy-cycle delay and may suppress a protective withdrawal as a tracking error. To address these challenges, we propose ARC (Ascending Reflex Control), a bottom-up framework that integrates instantaneous tactile reflexes with learned whole-body control. ARC consists of two components: an instantaneous reflex pathway and bottom-up reflex integration. The reflex pathway detects hazardous contacts from full-body tactile sensing, solves a whole-body withdrawal pose, and delivers it directly to the motors within 10 ms. Bottom-up reflex integration combines reflex-in-the-loop policy learning, reflex-transparent policy alignment, and reflex-informed policy adaptation to sustain the withdrawal, maintain balance, and complete longer-horizon recovery. We deploy ARC on a Unitree G1 and evaluate three categories of hazardous contact. Compared with an otherwise identical reflex delayed by 20 ms, ARC reduces the first force peak by 34.1% and reduces the contact impulse from 0.2632 N s to 0.1225 N s (a 2.15x ratio). We further demonstrate protected motion tracking, teleoperation, and vision-free obstacle traversal guided by foot tactile sensing. Project page: https://minusmodulo.github.io/reflexarc-website/

papers.title: Reality and Perceptual Gaps in Expressive Swarm Robotics
papers.authors: Ali Imran, Abdalwhab Bakheet Mohammed Abdalwhab, Rafael Gomes Braga, Hélène Duval, Audrey Rochette, Vivek Shankar Varadharajan, Yann Bouteiller, Jean Mazerolle, et al.
papers.abstract: Moving robot swarms from simulation into the physical world can be difficult because small discrepancies in hardware, timing and communication can cascade across interacting robots and alter group behaviour. This challenge is known as the reality gap. When swarms operate in human environments, a second challenge emerges: a perceptual gap between what the swarm physically does and what human onlookers actually perceive. This study examines the same decentralised coordination code deployed across three robotic swarms-tabletop, aerial and human-scale mobile manipulators-during live artistic performances. We find that while the underlying algorithms executed reliably on all three platforms, physical embodiment drastically altered visible motion-distorting execution timescales by more than a factor of three and reshaping trajectory geometry. More importantly, audience surveys revealed that human interpretation does not mirror technical success: how observers attribute meaning (perceived purpose) and how they react emotionally (comfort versus threat) depend heavily on physical form. Meaning attribution and emotional responses did not vary together. Our results demonstrate that successfully transferring swarm software to physical hardware is insufficient for real-world deployment. Addressing the reality gap does not guarantee that the resulting collective motion will be readily interpreted by human observers. Swarms destined for human environments must be engineered not only for decentralised stability but also for the expressive physical dynamics through which humans interpret collective motion.

papers.title: RAIPAL: A Powerful and Agile Humanoid Arm for Human Tasks
papers.authors: Donggeon Kim, Hyungho Chris Choi, Donghyuk Choi, Jeongsoo Park, Choongin Lee, Chan Park, Jemin Hwangbo
papers.abstract: This paper presents humanoid manipulator hardware designed specifically for human-level performance throughout its broad domain of tasks, from heavy payloads to highly dynamic motions. Unlike conventional designs targeting uniform workspace capability, the proposed approach derives force, speed, and endurance targets from published measurements of task-relevant human upper-limb performance. These targets guide the actuator, mechanism, and thermal design toward torque transparency and sustained operation. The platform integrates force-oriented upper-arm components, speed-oriented forearm components, and a posture-dependent elbow mechanism that shifts its torque-speed behavior. These components are driven by planetary actuators and compact actuator-embedded electronics. Experimental results validate broad task capability, demonstrating a peak payload of 20 kg (2.25x its own mass), an endpoint speed of 20.6 m/s, and continued operation under repeated hammering impacts. Thermal analysis further confirms that the robot's sustained operation capability exceeds the published human load--duration boundary across nearly the entire load spectrum. These findings show that hardware targets derived from human-task measurements narrow the human-to-humanoid capability gap. A supplementary video is available at https://youtu.be/xVUWFICD5G0

papers.title: RAFT: Reasoning-Aligned Fine-Tuning Improves Robustness of VLA Post-Training
papers.authors: Shresth Grover, Andrey Kolobov, Dhruv Shah
papers.abstract: Adapting a generalist vision-language-action (VLA) policy to a target task with limited demonstrations can improve nominal task success while reducing robustness to variations in appearance, objects, and instructions. We introduce reasoning-aligned fine-tuning (RAFT), a two-stage post-training procedure: RAFT first trains low-rank adapters on task-relevant reasoning annotations, then freezes them while fine-tuning the policy on action demonstrations. On a physical DROID robot, RAFT achieves $75.0\%$ out-of-distribution success, compared with $27.9\%$ for plain fine-tuning; on a multi-stage bimanual YAM task, it reaches $70.0\%$ mean success, compared with $36.0\%$ for the strongest baseline. RAFT also improves success under visual, object, and instruction shifts in simulated pick-and-place and open-drawer tasks. Compared with plain fine-tuning, RAFT policies place more attention on annotated task regions and yield higher linear-probe accuracy for object identity in later layers. A broader reasoning-data mixture further improves downstream success across demonstration budgets.

papers.title: PyRUA-DataFarm: LLM Agent as a Cost-Efficient Teleoperator for Real-Ready Robot Data
papers.authors: Kewei Zhang, Juncheng Ma, Guodong Lv, Duomin Wang, Feixiang Ruan, Ruiyang Si, Chuanrui Zhang, Yuxuan Chen, et al.
papers.abstract: Teleoperation remains the default way to collect robot demonstrations, but every episode costs robot and operator time, and every new task starts from scratch. We ask whether a coding agent can take over the teleoperator's job. In our DataFarm, the agent receives a data request and one calibration episode of the robot in the target scene and rebuilds the task in simulation: it writes the scene, an expert controller, and a success judge. The simulator supplies exact actions, and a video model conditioned on real images renders each rollout as photographic video, generating all camera views together consistently. The output is real-ready data: synchronized camera views labelled with the robot's actions, on which a policy can be trained directly and deployed on the real robot. Independent judges certify the expert and every rendered episode before admission. On five real-robot tasks, policies trained only on farm data match policies trained on as many teleoperated episodes (93 vs. 84 successes in 100 trials), and under an unseen tablecloth and coloured light they keep 87 successes where the teleoperation-trained policies fall to 46. Adapting a task is fully automatic and costs \$21 of API usage on average, paid once per task, plus \$5 for a render contract; every further episode costs \$0.80 on average for simulation, rendering, and review, with no robot or operator. One hour of three-view data for a task costs \$107 on average, these costs included, slightly below a quote of \$117 for teleoperation in China and below \$290 in labour alone in North America.

papers.title: PrimeSim: A Generalist World Model Simulator from Large-Scale Cross-Embodiment Demonstrations
papers.authors: Travis Davies, Wentao Ma, Lihao Guo, Tengfei Ma, Xiaowen Chang, Jiafeng Xu, Shilong Wang, Yiqi Deng, et al.
papers.abstract: A robot world model that serves as a simulator must do more than generate plausible videos: it must faithfully follow commanded actions, maintain consistency across camera views, and sustain coherent long-horizon rollouts. We present PrimeSim, an action-conditioned, multiview world model simulator that addresses these challenges through progressive midtraining and posttraining. Starting from a pretrained video generator, we midtrain on 30,110 hours of robot demonstrations spanning 22 platforms. To improve action following, we introduce a unified cross-embodiment action representation and frame-aligned dual-path conditioning to strengthen action-frame correspondence. To maintain multiview consistency, we develop view-aware interleaved attention with explicit camera identities, enabling cross-view information exchange while preserving view-specific representations. We further introduce a fast-video, slow-memory posttraining framework that transforms the bidirectional video generator into an efficient autoregressive simulator. By combining fast causal generation, self-rollout training, and hierarchical temporal memory, PrimeSim mitigates error accumulation from self-generated histories and supports coherent long-horizon simulation. PrimeSim runs at 10.1 FPS, remains stable over long-horizon rollouts on rigid and deformable manipulation tasks, and transfers to held-out platforms within 100 to 200 gradient steps where the pretrained backbone does not. Against five open-source action-conditioned world models it leads four of the five WorldSimProbe suites and posts the best overall EWMBench score, while fine-grained local calibration still trails the field; its rollouts are faithful enough to support GRPO-based policy optimization. We release the model weights, inference code, and training code.

papers.title: PolicyIK: High-Precision Inverse Kinematics for Robot Arms with Reinforcement Learning
papers.authors: Yuhan Liu, Xinqi Liu, Zixuan Dong, Keith W. Ross, Shenji Wan
papers.abstract: Inverse kinematics (IK) converts end-effector pose commands into joint motion, and many vision-language-action (VLA) policies rely on it to act on a given arm and to transfer across embodiments. Precise IK remains laborious: redundancy and singularities complicate the inverse mapping, execution depends on hand-tuned controllers, and training data on physical robots are costly to collect. We present PolicyIK, a goal-conditioned reinforcement learning policy for high-precision IK. It updates joint-position references from pose feedback and observes its accumulated reference relative to the measured joints, so it can retain the offset that the position controller needs at rest. Two-scale pose errors with an error-dependent action gain resolve millimeter residuals while preserving large motions. Progress and dwell rewards teach it to both reach the tolerance and stay within it. In simulation, a single attempt by the trained PPO policy keeps the mean errors over the final second within 1 mm and 0.2° on 93.5% of held-out tasks, and a deployment protocol raises success to 98.9%. When trained directly on a physical arm with an off-policy RL learner, PolicyIK achieves higher reaching and holding success than all four classical IK controllers under the same time budgets. In simulated pick-and-place, PolicyIK executes the end-effector commands of the $π_{0.5}$ VLA policy with 95.7% success. These results show that reinforcement learning can provide high-precision inverse kinematics for robot arms. Code is available at https://github.com/Tinaliu0123/PolicyIK.

papers.title: Play Beyond Vision: Children’s Embodied Strategies in Non-Visual Extended Reality
papers.authors: Jules A. M. van Gurp, Giulia Cosentino, Isabella Possaghi, Noah Teglvang Sejer Iversen, Michail N. Giannakos, Panos Markopoulos, Sebastian Cmentowski
papers.abstract: Extended Reality (XR) enables play, learning, and social experiences, yet, the field remains dominated by an understanding of XR as a primarily vision-based technology. For children, this visual focus may introduce challenges such as uncomfortable headsets, excessive immersion, social withdrawal, and reduced shared play. We propose non-visual XR as a new design space for immersive experiences without visual augmentation, where virtual elements are conveyed through spatial audio, haptics, and embodied orientation. We investigate how children experience a sense of “being there” without relying on sight, and how they imagine interacting with invisible virtual elements. We conducted an exploratory study with 38 children consisting of two activities: a playful non-visual XR probe in which children located and chased an invisible ghost using custom-made wearables, and an elicitation activity in which children imagined interaction concepts within a Wizard-of-Oz setup. Our analysis shows how children interacted and envisioned non‑visual interactions using movement to sense and interpret non‑visual XR, relying on multimodal cues to anchor their understanding. As contributions, we provide an empirical characterization of a non‑visual XR game for children and distilled lessons for designing and researching future non-visual XR play experiences.

papers.title: Physical Diffusion Policy via MPM-Guided 3D Gaussian Simulation
papers.authors: Can Wang, Qiyuan Qiao, Lei Liu, Ge Yuan, Xinhui Liu, Dong Xu
papers.abstract: Learning robust manipulation policies for diverse everyday objects remains challenging because objects with different materials exhibit distinct deformation and contact dynamics. While diffusion policies provide a powerful framework for modeling multimodal manipulation behaviors, they typically lack explicit physical reasoning and may produce averaged actions when facing heterogeneous objects. We present a physics-aware diffusion policy that augments visual imitation learning with object physical understanding. Our framework recovers material properties from visual demonstrations by coupling 3D Gaussian Splatting with differentiable Material Point Method simulation, where video guidance and particle-level constraints enable accurate physical parameter estimation. The estimated physics conditions are further integrated into a material-aware Mixture-of-Experts diffusion policy, allowing adaptive behavior generation across different physical regimes. For practical deployment, we introduce a physics memory bank that provides efficient physical retrieval without requiring online simulation optimization. Experiments on a wide range of simulated and real-world objects demonstrate improved manipulation success and generalization over existing diffusion-based approaches. These results show that incorporating physical knowledge is critical for scalable robot manipulation in diverse environments.

papers.title: Physical AI Security: A Unified Five-Layer Taxonomy for a Systematic Survey from Silicon to Semantics
papers.authors: Ahmed M. Elmisery, Nabil Moukafih, Suga Junichi
papers.abstract: Collaborative robots, autonomous mobile robots (AMRs), and edge inference nodes inside Industrial Control Systems (ICS) now let AI models drive physical actuators. For these systems a cyberattack is no longer only a data problem: a successful exploit can disrupt infrastructure, halt production, or injure people. Research on Physical AI Security (PAIS) is split across hardware trust, artificial intelligence, robotics, operational technology, and cyber-physical systems, which makes it hard to see how risks and defenses depend on one another across the cycle of AI-driven sensing, decision-making, actuation, and feedback. We propose a five-layer taxonomy for PAIS: hardware-rooted trust, pre-deployment validation, runtime assurance, domain semantics, and knowledge feedback. The taxonomy is organized around the physical decision and gives the fragmented literature a common structure in which cross-layer dependencies can be stated. Using it as the classification frame, we conduct a PRISMA-informed structured review of 312 primary papers published between 2015 and 2025 across six databases, supplemented by 28 standards, 14 regulatory frameworks, and 12 incident reports. Existing work covers individual layers well but does little to connect them across the Physical AI lifecycle. Coverage is thinnest exactly where Physical AI differs most from classical ICS: model provenance, validation of learned controllers, and human-robot interaction security. From these gaps we derive a prioritized agenda of ten research challenges and an unevaluated reference architecture with falsifiable evaluation criteria. The taxonomy is offered as a shared frame for organizing the field, assessing where existing approaches fall short, and directing work toward secure and resilient Physical AI systems.

papers.title: PACT: Pose-Robust Actuation Co-Design for Tendon-Driven Robotic Hands
papers.authors: Prashant Kumar, Rachael Granberry, Taylor Niehues, Andrew A. Stanley, Gabe Pirie
papers.abstract: Humanoid robotic hands must provide sufficient force, speed, and backdrivability within a human-scale envelope. Tendon-driven transmissions address this challenge by relocating actuators to the palm and forearm, but routing paths, moment arms, and capstan dimensions jointly determine both force capability and joint speed, so selecting them sequentially satisfies one requirement at the expense of the other. This paper presents a pose-robust actuation co-design for tendon-driven robot hands (PACT) framework that optimizes tendon routing, moment arms, and capstan dimensions under pose-dependent force requirements and drivetrain-bandwidth constraints. A feasible-force formulation enforces actuator bounds and equilibrium at all joints, while a max-min objective maximizes task-force coverage at the weakest pose. Applied to a four-degree-of-freedom finger, the framework produces an asymmetric N + 1 tendon topology using quasi-direct-drive actuators. Across eight poses, the design achieves task-force coverage of 0.88-1.00 and a predicted 5 Hz minimum isolated-joint flexion/extension bandwidth within a 70th-percentile human-size envelope. Prototype measurements deviate from predictions by up to 24.5%, primarily due to unmodeled transmission losses. These results indicate that co-designing routing with the drivetrain can meet pose-dependent force requirements without relaxing the bandwidth constraint, paving the way for human-sized robotic hands with human-level performance.

papers.title: Online iLQR-MPC with Whole-Body Control for Robust Humanoid Locomotion
papers.authors: Xiang Li, Linlin Ou, Ruihan Wu, Xinyi Yu
papers.abstract: Humanoid locomotion requires deciding where to step and how to distribute contact forces. However, a disturbance can invalidate the nominal plan, requiring coordinated revision under constraints that switch with every footfall. To solve this online, the proposed approach employs the single-rigid-body model, which retains attitude dynamics and the full contact wrench. An iterative linear-quadratic-regulator MPC (iLQR-MPC) then jointly optimizes contact forces and footstep locations in a single receding-horizon problem, without a separate step planner. Specifically, contact and motion constraints are incorporated into the backward pass through augmented-Lagrangian and relaxed-barrier penalties. A whole-body controller subsequently maps the plan to joint torques at 500 Hz while preserving contact feasibility. The model-based formulation makes disturbance responses interpretable through explicit costs and constraints, and requires no platform-specific policy training. In MuJoCo simulations, the iLQR-MPC replans at 100 Hz (mean solve time 8.9 ms); the Unitree G1 sustains steady-state walking and recovers from impulsive 245 N forward and 175 N lateral pushes.

papers.title: Online Hamilton-Jacobi Reachability Onboard the Robot Control Loop: A Real-Time GPU Solver for Safety-Critical Autonomy
papers.authors: Kevin Weekly, Alexandre M. Bayen
papers.abstract: Hamilton-Jacobi (HJ) reachability provides certified backward reachable tubes (BRTs) for safety-critical robotic systems, but the level-set computation scales exponentially in the state dimension and has historically been performed offline. As autonomy stacks (ADAS/AV, humanoid robotics, and vision-language-action models) increasingly rely on black-box, probabilistic policies, a deterministic safety layer with formal guarantees is an essential complement. We present a CUDA implementation of the canonical WENO5 + TVD-RK3 + Lax-Friedrichs level-set Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs solver for 2D, 3D, and 4D dynamics that is fast enough to run inside a robot's control loop. In 32-bit floating point (FP32) on a single workstation GPU (NVIDIA RTX 4000 Ada), it computes the 3D Air3D BRT at 112 Hz, a 4D pursuit-evasion BRT at 61 Hz, and a 2D wind-affected drifter BRT at 74-147 Hz, 5.9-17.5x faster than the JAX reference hj_reachability at matched precision and 1.7-16x faster than a torch.compile reimplementation of the same scheme. In 64-bit floating point (FP64) it agrees with hj_reachability on eight benchmark cases, reproduces Mitchell's Air3D BRT to within 0.04% of the reference cell count, and runs 2.0-4.6x faster. On an embedded NVIDIA Jetson AGX Thor it computes Air3D at 66 Hz (N=41) and the 2D drifter at 54 Hz, 3.8-8.9x faster than hj_reachability on the same device. As a multi-agent application, an in-kernel label-propagation extension recovers the K-agent capture-basin Voronoi tessellation from a single combined HJ solve, independent of fleet size; it runs at 4.0 ms per tick in a closed-loop wildfire-response simulation of six quadcopters under time-varying, non-uniform wind.

papers.title: OdorSpaces: Visual-Olfactory Embodied Navigation in 3D Environments
papers.authors: Changyeon Lee, Kelin Yu, Zheng Wei, Shuna Ni, Ruohan Gao
papers.abstract: Olfaction provides critical information about airborne chemical cues, yet it remains largely underexplored in embodied AI, with limited prior machine olfaction work focusing primarily on semantic odor perception. We introduce OdorSpaces, a physics-based simulation platform and benchmark for visual-olfactory embodied navigation. OdorSpaces augments Habitat-Sim with 3D odor transport and dispersion simulated by Fire Dynamics Simulator (FDS), enabling agents to navigate photorealistic indoor environments using both visual and olfactory observations. The benchmark includes two representative source-seeking scenarios: invisible gas-leak localization and early-stage fire localization. We develop an initial multimodal reinforcement learning policy that integrates visual observations and olfactory measurements over time. Experiments show that the policy outperforms a diverse set of baselines, establishing a strong reference for future research on visual-olfactory embodied navigation.

papers.title: Neurotechnology, Human Cognition, and Ethical Challenges in Emerging Digital Futures
papers.authors: Ahmed Khan, Ayesha Malik
papers.abstract: Neurotechnology refers to the integration of neuroscience, biomedical engineering, computer science, artificial intelligence, and digital technologies that help interact with, analyze, interpret, or modulate neural activity. Thanks to innovations in brain-computer interfaces, signal processing, neurostimulation, wearable devices, and artificial intelligence, neurotechnology goes beyond traditional clinical uses and moves into cognition assistance, rehabilitation, communication, human-computer interaction, and new digital realms. These innovations offer immense opportunities for advancing healthcare and aiding people suffering from neurological disabilities; at the same time, they pose complex ethical, legal, social, and security issues. This paper explores the background, application, emerging trends, ethical issues, and regulation needs of neurotechnology. This paper discusses cognitive enhancement, cognitive restoration, decision-making, autonomy, identity, and human-technology interactions. Intersections of neurotechnology, artificial intelligence, the Internet of Things, and immersive digital environments and increasing financial value of neural data are also discussed. Specific focus is placed on mental privacy, informed consent, cognitive liberty, equal access, cybersecurity, manipulation, and responsible innovation. Conceptual governance framework is introduced, which incorporates privacy, security, ethical assessment, human control, and responsibility throughout technology lifecycle. This analysis stresses importance of developing proper mechanisms to accompany technological development to ensure human dignity and autonomy. In conclusion, interdisciplinary research, adaptive governance, security of neural data, and human-oriented design are needed to make sure that neurotechnology develops safely, responsibly, inclusively, and socially valuable way in the future.

papers.title: Nested Field-of-View Barriers for Teleoperated Multi-Robot Relay Chains
papers.authors: Arthur Vangasse, Theo Cruz, Thales Soares, André Cid, Vinícius Gonçalves, Gustavo Freitas, Luciano Pimenta
papers.abstract: Teleoperation of mobile robots in communication-denied environments requires maintaining a communication link while allowing the operator to maneuver freely. We propose a shared-autonomy framework in which a teleoperated leader is followed by a chain of autonomous robots that relays a line of sight to a fixed base station, a geometric proxy for the link. Connectivity is enforced geometrically through visibility-based Control Barrier Functions (CBFs), with each agent computing its control input locally through a quadratic program. A strict visibility constraint guarantees connectivity, but a follower with no independent motion objective remains stationary, stalling the leader at the boundary of the safe set. Relaxing it preserves mobility at the cost of the guarantee. Our framework resolves this conflict through nested hard-soft visibility constraints: a full field-of-view (FoV) constraint enforced strictly to guarantee connectivity and a contracted FoV constraint imposed on each follower as a relaxed behavioral objective that drives it inward before the connectivity boundary is reached. We prove feasibility of the local quadratic programs and forward invariance of the connected, collision-free set under the resulting distributed controller. The contraction parameter shapes follower behavior without affecting the guarantee, which follows from the strict constraint alone. The framework is evaluated in confined and cluttered environments on two simulated systems: a kinematic integrator and software-in-the-loop Crazyflie quadrotors. Compared with a baseline tuned to reach the goal in comparable time, the framework keeps the links far closer to the connected set and moves the followers less.

papers.title: Neighborhood-Aware Fuzzy Rough Action Selection for Vision-Language-Action Manipulation
papers.authors: Mengqi Mao, Xiangjian Chen, Shixin Huang
papers.abstract: Abstract Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models map visual observations and language instructions to robot actions, but the highest-scoring action is not always the most reliable one for physical execution. A candidate may satisfy the language instruction and remain collision-free at its nominal pose, while nearby actions exhibit less favorable physical properties. We present FRS-Grounding, a fuzzy rough set-based action-selection framework that evaluates each VLA candidate together with its local execution structure. Given a finite candidate set, FRS-Grounding combines a normalized VLA-conditioned candidate score and a physical-distance value to form a semantic–physical fuzzy action set. Pairwise translational and rotational differences, together with collision-free states, define a physics-informed fuzzy action relation. Fuzzy rough lower and upper approximations are then used to characterize local support within the candidate set. Candidates with stronger neighborhood-consistent support are distinguished from those lying in the boundary region, and these regions are mapped to normal execution, compliant execution, or rejection. Across 1500 randomized simulation trials, FRS-Grounding achieves a success rate of 86.4% and a safety-violation rate of 2.1%, compared with 74.8% and 8.2% for VLA-HC. Its semantic compliance is 0.89, close to RT-2 (0.91) and higher than VoxPoser (0.85) and VLA-HC (0.88). Under positional noise with σ = 10 mm, FRS-Grounding retains a success rate of approximately 78%, compared with approximately 28% for VLA-HC. Real-robot experiments further show how the boundary branch can be coupled with force-compliant control. The results support candidate-set evaluation as a practical way to combine VLA preferences with local physical structure in the tested manipulation tasks.

papers.title: Mass Scaling Laws for Energy-Optimal Horizontal Multirotor Flight
papers.authors: Ayush Patnaik, Nicolas Michel, Leonard Baursfeld, Davide Scaramuzza, Xinfan Lin
papers.abstract: Multicopters are a type of aerial robot seeing extensive real-world applications but with range and endurance as critical bottlenecks. Optimization of its energy efficiency through energy-aware flight planning (e.g. cruise speed-scheduling) has hence been an important topic. The mass of the multicopter is an important factor to consider, as it has a significant impact on efficiency, and many common applications are subject to frequent mass variation due to payload change. This work derives closed-form scaling relationships between the energy-optimal steady horizontal flight behavior of a multicopter and its vehicle mass, and validates them experimentally on two multirotor platforms. Specifically, for mass-only variation, i.e., when payload changes the vehicle mass while the airframe geometry, aerodynamic characteristics, and rotor configuration remain unchanged, we show through a combination of numerical simulation, theoretical derivation, and experimental validation that (1) the energy-optimal velocity is proportional to the square root of vehicle mass; (2) the energy-optimal pitch angle is constant with respect to mass; and (3) the optimal energy per meter is proportional to mass. The analysis shows that these three relationships arise from a common mass-similarity property of the steady-state flight and rotor-aerodynamic equations. Furthermore, the obtained scaling relationships enable simple yet effective cruise-speed planning to optimize energy efficiency and extend the range and endurance of the multicopter.
